messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 65
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Special Education Teacher
- Trauma Type: Military
- Pcl5: 35

He is 65 now, a special education teacher who has spent most of his adult life helping children who startle easily, struggle to trust, or need the world explained with patience and repetition. In the classroom, he is known for his calm voice and careful routines. He dims the fluorescent lights when they are too much for a student, gives warnings before the fire drill, and never stands too close behind a child’s chair. His colleagues see him as steady and kind. What they do not see is how deliberately he has built his life around avoiding surprise.

He grows up in a Latin American family where duty is spoken of with reverence and fear is something a man is expected to swallow. When he is a young man, he enters the military believing it will give him structure, purpose, and a way to support his family. At first he tells the story in broad strokes, as if reading from a script he has repeated for decades. Then the details begin to come. There is an attack that happens fast and without warning. He remembers heat, smoke, the metallic smell of blood, and the stunned expression on the face of a fellow soldier just before he collapses. He remembers trying to move, trying to help, and realizing in the same moment that he might die there too. Later, what stays with him most is not only terror but helplessness—the feeling of being trapped inside a scene that keeps unfolding no matter what he does.

When he comes home, people treat survival as if it should be enough. He tries to do the same. He tells very little to his family. He learns to speak about the military in polished, impersonal fragments. Inside, though, the attack does not stay in the past. For years he sleeps lightly, waking at small sounds with his heart already pounding. If a car backfires, his body reacts before his mind catches up; his shoulders tense, his breath shortens, and for a split second he is no longer on a city street. He avoids war movies, avoids crowded celebrations with fireworks, avoids conversations with other veterans who “want to reminisce.” He says he just prefers quiet.

His marriage slowly organizes itself around what he cannot tolerate. He checks the locks more than once before bed. He insists on sitting where he can see the door in restaurants. He becomes irritable over things that seem minor even to him—an unexpected touch from behind, a pan dropped in the kitchen, his children shouting during play. He hates the sharpness in his own voice when he snaps at them. At night his ex-wife sometimes wakes him because he is yelling in his sleep, arms flung up as if bracing for impact. When she asks what he was dreaming, he says he does not remember, though often he does: smoke, shouting, someone calling for help, his own body refusing to move fast enough. Over time she experiences him as distant, unreachable. He experiences himself as failing at ordinary family life for reasons he cannot explain without feeling weak or ashamed. After the divorce, he tells people they simply grew apart.

Teaching becomes the part of life that makes the most sense. In special education, he can turn vigilance into competence. He notices every change in a child’s posture, every sign that a meltdown is building, every sound in the hallway that may throw the room off balance. Students respond to his predictability. He never raises his voice unless absolutely necessary, and when a student is overwhelmed, he is the one who remains in the room, speaking softly, helping the child orient to the present. Yet the same school environment also strains him. Fire drills leave him trembling afterward in the staff bathroom, splashing water on his face until the shaking settles. When a student slams a door, he feels a surge of anger and fear so intense that he has to grip the edge of his desk. He is embarrassed by how long it takes for his body to understand that he is safe.

Now, in his mid-sixties, he lives alone. He keeps the television on low in the evenings because silence lets memories get louder. He avoids sleep, then resents his exhaustion. Some mornings he arrives at school already worn thin after a night of broken rest and dreams he cannot fully shake. He describes feeling “on guard all the time,” as if some part of him never stood down after the military. He is troubled by how often he thinks of the men who did not come home and by the stubborn belief that he should have done more, reacted faster, been different somehow. He knows this thought is not entirely rational, but it remains.

In session, he does not present as dramatic. He is courteous, contained, almost formal. But when he speaks about the attack, his gaze fixes on a point just beyond the room and his hands tighten around each other. He says he has spent a lifetime being dependable for everyone else. What is harder to admit is that, despite the decades that have passed, part of him is still living in that moment of smoke and noise, waiting for the next explosion.
